t: Minimum Lines to Represent a Line Chart
o: Points must be visited in day order, so sort by day first. Consecutive collinear runs share one line; the answer is 1 plus the number of times the slope between consecutive points changes. Example 1 has slopes -1,-1,-1,0,-1,-1,-1 → changes at the flat segment and after it → 3 lines. Example 2 sorts to a perfectly straight line → 1 line. Coordinates go up to 1e9, so comparing floating-point slopes risks precision errors — compare cross products instead.
k: Sort points by day; adjacency in the chart follows sorted order.
Collinearity of three consecutive points is dx1*dy2 == dx2*dy1 (exact integer math).
Answer = number of slope changes + 1 (or 0 for a single point).

a.i: After sorting, walk consecutive triples; whenever (p[i]-p[i-1]) and (p[i+1]-p[i]) are not parallel, a new line starts. Parallelism via cross product avoids any division.
s: If fewer than 2 points, return n-1.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the scan is O(n).

a.i: Compare (dy/dx) of adjacent segments as doubles with a small tolerance. Intuitive, but products up to 1e18 exceed exact double precision, so equal slopes of huge coordinates can be misjudged — acceptable here only because tests are mild.
s: Compute slope of each segment as a double.
Count positions where the slope differs from the previous beyond 1e-9.

w: Always prefer the cross-product version: it is exact and immune to precision issues. Common bugs: forgetting to sort (example 2 is deliberately shuffled), mishandling n=1 (answer 0) and n=2 (answer 1), and integer overflow in 32-bit cross products (use 64-bit). Follow-up: minimum lines for a piecewise-linear approximation under error tolerance would need convex-hull-style machinery.
